title: Arjuna's Despair and Collapse
story:
The two armies had drawn up on the plain of Kurukshetra, and the war everyone had dreaded and prepared for was about to begin. Years of grievance and humiliation had been folded into this single hour. Every man on that field was someone's father, son, or brother; almost all of them shared the same blood. Then, before a single arrow flew, the man at its center lost the will to fight.

The Kauravas and the Pandavas stood facing each other, and the sound of their conches and drums and cymbals and horns filled the field. Duryodhana had walked the length of his own army naming its warriors to his preceptor Drona — Bhishma, Karna, Kripa, Aswatthaman — and the venerable old grandsire Bhishma had raised his conch and blown a lion's roar. On the other side, standing on a great chariot yoked to white steeds, Krishna blew the conch Panchajanya and Arjuna blew Devadatta. The terrible Bhima blew his great conch Paundra, Yudhishthira blew Anantavijaya, and Nakula and Sahadeva blew Sughosa and Manipushpaka. The answering horns went up, and for a moment the whole plain was one vast, brazen noise.

And then Arjuna looked across the field, and everything stopped.

He saw the men arrayed before him, his own kinsmen on both sides. There was his grandsire Bhishma, the venerable old warrior who had presided over his whole life. There was his preceptor Drona, who had taught him the bow. There was Karna and Kripa and Aswatthaman, and beyond them cousins and kinsmen he had grown up beside, uncles and nephews and the sons of old friends. And behind him, in his own ranks, stood Subhadra's son, his own boy, and the sons of Draupadi. These were the men the war had gathered — and the men he was about to kill.

The pity came on him all at once, and it was not a small thing. His body began to tremble, and the hair stood on end along his skin, and his skin burned. It was not fear that did this; it was something nearer to love, and it was stronger than either. The great bow Gandiva, which had never failed him, slipped from his fingers — and with it slipped everything he had prepared for this day. He could not hold it. A man who cannot raise his bow cannot fight a war, and this man had been the hope of an entire side of it.

He spoke, despondent, to Krishna beside him. His voice, which had carried across a hundred battlefields, was low. 'I wish not to slay these though they slay me,' he said. 'O slayer of Madhu.' What kind of victory, he was asking without quite asking, would be bought with the deaths of his own people?

He did not wait for an answer, or perhaps he could not. His mind troubled with grief, he cast aside his bow and his arrows and sat down in the chariot, right there on the field of battle, between two armies that were waiting for him. The conches that had roared a moment before were silent; the field held its breath. The noise of the day fell away, and the man who was supposed to lead them all sat slumped and still.

Krishna did not speak yet. He held the reins, and he waited. There would be time for words soon, and the words would change everything. But for now there was only this: the strongest man on the field, undone not by any enemy but by the sight of the people he loved standing where he would have to kill them.
reflection: The Gita does not begin with philosophy; it begins with a man falling apart. Before Krishna can teach Arjuna anything, Arjuna has to be honest about what he feels — and what he feels is that the victory he has spent his life preparing for is not worth the faces in front of him.
next_story_tease: But Krishna had not yet spoken — and what he was about to say would become the heart of the teaching.
hero_scene: Arjuna slumped in his chariot on the field of Kurukshetra, the great bow Gandiva slipped from his hand and his arrows cast aside, while Krishna stands quietly at the reins against the hush of two waiting armies.
